summary: This standards-track document defines a YANG data model for managing network interfaces, covering both configuration and system state. It is meant as a generic base that interface-type-specific models can extend. It is written to work with the Network Management Datastore Architecture.

plainLanguage.summary: Every computer has plug-in points to the network. This is a standard form for describing and checking each one, which other forms can add details to.

subtitle: A common YANG model for listing, configuring and monitoring the network interfaces on a device.

tldr.problem: Network interfaces are central to many Internet protocols, so management systems need one common way to identify, configure and monitor them.
tldr.mechanism: The ietf-interfaces YANG module defines a flat list of interfaces keyed by name, with configuration leaves, read-only status leaves and traffic counters. Interface-type-specific models augment it.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 7223 by moving all read-only data into the /interfaces tree to fit the Network Management Datastore Architecture, and it deprecates /interfaces-state.

today: RFC 8343 is a Proposed Standard and replaces RFC 7223. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and RFC 8344 builds on it for IP configuration.

sections.title: Why a Common Interface Model
sections.content:
RFC 8343 defines a YANG data model for managing network interfaces. It contains configuration data and state data, which means status information plus counters for collecting statistics. The RFC expects interface-type-specific models to augment this generic one.

The reason is that interfaces are central to the management of many Internet protocols, so it is important to have a common data model for how they are identified, configured and monitored. This version supports the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA) from RFC 8342.

It obsoletes RFC 7223. The main change is that the /interfaces-state subtree is deprecated and all config false data nodes now live in /interfaces. Servers that do not implement NMDA, or that serve clients that do not, MAY still implement the deprecated tree.
sections.plainLanguage: Lots of network programs need to talk about the same plug-in points. This RFC gives everyone one shared way to name and check them.

sections.title: Design Objectives
sections.content:
The RFC lists what the model is meant to achieve. It should be simple enough for existing products to map onto their own native models, and also usable as is by new implementations. A reference to an interface should be as simple as possible, preferably a single leafref.

The mapping to ifIndex, the identifier used by SNMP, must be clear. The model must support interface layering: one interface on top of exactly one other, or one interface formed by aggregating N others, or N interfaces multiplexed over one.

It should also support pre-provisioning, meaning configuring an interface whose hardware is not present, and both physical and logical interfaces. Finally it includes read-only counters for sent and received octets and packets, received packets with errors, and packets that could not be sent due to errors.
sections.plainLanguage: The goal is a form that is easy to fill in, works for real and pretend plug-in points, and keeps score of what goes in and out.

sections.title: The Interface List
sections.content:
The module ietf-interfaces uses a flat list at /interfaces/interface. Each entry is identified by its name and has a mandatory type. Types are identities, and the iana-if-type module from RFC 7224 defines identities for the IANA ifType registry.

Configuration leaves include description, enabled (default true) and, with the if-mib feature, link-up-down-trap-enable. Read-only leaves include oper-status, last-change, phys-address, speed, and with if-mib also admin-status and if-index.

The oper-status values are up, down, testing, unknown, dormant, not-present and lower-layer-down. The statistics container holds discontinuity-time and in and out counters for octets, unicast, broadcast and multicast packets, discards and errors, plus in-unknown-protos.

Other modules point at interfaces with the interface-ref typedef, which refers to an interface by its name. The RFC says other modules SHOULD use it.
sections.plainLanguage: The list is like a roll call of plug-in points, each with a name, a kind, an on/off switch and a scoreboard.

sections.title: System-Controlled and User-Controlled Interfaces
sections.content:
A system-controlled interface is created and deleted by the system regardless of configuration. Examples are hardware that appears when a line card is added, or a loopback interface that appears when the IP stack is enabled. A user-controlled interface exists because explicit configuration was added, such as a VLAN interface on an Ethernet interface.

When the system creates an interface, it tries to apply the intended configuration that has the same name. If there is none, or the configured type does not match the real type, it creates the interface without applying explicit configuration.

If a device supports arbitrarily named user-controlled interfaces it advertises the arbitrary-names feature. Without it, names MUST match the device's naming scheme. The pre-provisioning feature signals that configuring an absent interface is allowed. Otherwise the server MAY reject configuration for a system-controlled interface that is not present, and a NETCONF server MUST reply with an rpc-error with error-tag invalid-value.
sections.plainLanguage: Some plug-in points show up by themselves, like a new gadget being plugged in. Others only exist because you wrote them down on the list.

sections.title: Layering and Extension
sections.content:
There is no generic mechanism to configure one interface on top of another. Interface-type-specific models define their own nodes for that, using interface-ref to point at lower layers. The RFC's example is a bonding model with a slave-if leaf-list restricted by a must expression to interfaces of type ethernetCsmacd.

The generic model offers a read-only view of the result through two leaf-lists, higher-layer-if and lower-layer-if.

Type-specific models augment the interface list and use a when condition on the type leaf, so that, for example, an ethernet container with a duplex leaf appears only for Ethernet interfaces. Appendices A to C give Ethernet, bonding and VLAN examples.
sections.plainLanguage: The main list does not say how to stack plug-in points. Other forms do that, and the main list only shows what is stacked on what.

sections.title: Relationship to the IF-MIB
sections.content:
If a device implements the IF-MIB from RFC 2863, each entry in the operational interface list typically maps to one ifEntry. The if-index leaf MUST contain that entry's ifIndex. The RFC provides a table, for example name to ifName, type to ifType, description to ifAlias and oper-status to ifOperStatus.

Some IF-MIB objects are not mapped: ifPromiscuousMode, ifMtu, ifDescr and ifConnectorPresent. MTU is left to type-specific models.

The IF-MIB has 32-bit and 64-bit counters, and the 64-bit versions were added for interfaces faster than 20,000,000 bits/second. This model provides only 64-bit counters for the octet and packet counts, so a server and an SNMP agent may differ in how often they refresh values.
sections.plainLanguage: Older tools used a different form. This RFC says which box on the new form matches which box on the old one.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The module is meant to be accessed with NETCONF or RESTCONF. The mandatory-to-implement secure transport is SSH for NETCONF and TLS for RESTCONF, and the NETCONF access control model from RFC 8341 can limit what each user may read or write.

Writable data nodes can be sensitive. The RFC names two: the /interfaces/interface list and its enabled leaf. Unauthorized access to either could cause the device to ignore packets it should receive and process.

For IANA, the RFC registers the URI urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-interfaces in the IETF XML Registry.
sections.plainLanguage: Switching a plug-in point off by mistake would make the device stop listening, so only trusted people should be allowed to flip those switches.
